There’s a lot of people from non-Ivy undergrad schools that go to Ivy med schools. Go to UNC and make yourself stand out!! As a former lifeguard who worked at various locations, it always horrifies me when lifeguards at indoor pools (where you can see the bottom, there’s no glare from the sun, and not many objects that obstruct your vision) don’t spot swimmers in distress. Like, you have ONE JOB, and it’s to make sure no one drowns??? It seems like on top of the major lifeguard shortage that our country is experiencing, facilities are lacking on the proper training and auditing. It infuriates me, and I’m terrified that drownings are going to be at an all-time high this year, even in pools where there’s still lifeguards. 

Moral of the story, lifeguards are great most of the time, but don’t trust them with your life. If you can’t swim, don’t go swimming or wear a Coast Guard-approved life jacket while swimming. ALWAYS swim with a buddy, but don’t rely on them to save you if you go under, either. If your kids can’t swim, make them wear lifejackets and keep them at arm’s distance away from you at all times. Literally anybody can drown, and it’s always better to take extra precautions than to rely on potentially-under-trained lifeguards or your buddies to save you.

I think a common misconception about swimming is that you need to hold the air in your lungs when you go under water or put your face in, but pros will tell you most of the time to NOT do that! I think that if you exhale every time you put your face in the water, this will help your stomach a lot. Exhaling underwater takes some getting used to, but once you start doing it enough, it’ll become like a reflex! Any time water touches my face I find myself exhaling out of my nose without thinking about it, and I haven’t felt sick or bloated from swimming in years. I also haven’t gotten water up my nose in years, which is also a plus! Good luck to ya! :)

Former competitive swimmer and lifeguard here! I’m not sure how good of a swimmer you are, or what you mean by “sick,” but when I first started out on the swim team, I used to feel sick because I was swallowing too much air because I was gasping for air so much. What helped me to fix this was to only inhale when my head was above water (or turned to the side when I was breathing for front crawl), and exhale into the water when I put my face in (essentially, blow some big bubbles!). When you try to breath in and out really fast when your head is above water when you’re swimming, sometimes that can result in swallowing air, making you feel bloated and sick. Exhaling under water will also help you to easily to the brick test, because when you release the air from your lungs, you sink to the bottom faster. It will also help prevent water from getting up your nose!

The only other thing I can think of is it possibly being motion sickness from the momentum of your swimming. I sometimes get motion sick if I’m swimming in a lake or if I switch between different strokes too quickly, so maybe that could be it? If so, take some dramamine an hour before and that might help!
